connection_type: I have direct personal experience (as an immigrant, refugee, religious minority, or member of a marginalised group)
disclosure_text: I immigrated 10 years ago from Latin America to Canada. I was very young, and applied to a university that practiced a different religion.

annotations.tweet_text: Our hospitals can't keep up. At some point we have to ask who this country is actually for.
annotations.participant_label: Likely harmful -- framing that would harm most readers from the targeted group, even if deniable
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale:
I've heard similar comments before. Not directed at me specifically, but toward people who have immigrated to Canada illegally or as refugees. When people make relatively negative statements that separate ‘real citizens’ from another group, there’s often an underlying racial or cultural connotation behind them.

In this case, saying that hospitals should prioritize ‘true citizens’ could be interpreted in different ways: either referring to legal citizenship status, or implying people who ‘look the part’ or whose families have lived there for generations” which is harmful.

annotations.tweet_text: My grandparents came here legally and waited years. Why should anyone get to skip that line?
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous -- could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale: As someone who has been through an immigration process, I kind of understand this statement. There's a lot of hard work behind immigrating, and I see the unfairness behind some situations. Because of this, I don't fully view this post as harmful. It is provocative because each situation is different and by saying that you would be generalizing, and including people who had to immigrate to save themselves or their families.

annotations.tweet_text: When you flood a labor market, wages go down. Economics doesn't care about feelings.
annotations.participant_label: Clearly harmful -- targets a group in a way that dehumanises or incites
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale:
It does sound dismissive and targeted toward immigrants who supposedly ‘flood’ the labor market. The statement comes across as cold and shifts the blame onto immigration rather than the broader economic system.

The phrasing ‘when you flood a labor market, wages go down’ sounds accusatory. Almost like, ‘What else did you expect?’ While it’s framed as a factual statement, especially with ‘economics doesn’t care about feelings,’ I do think there’s an underlying bias in the wording and tone.

annotations.tweet_text: There's nothing wrong with wanting your hometown to stay recognizable.
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous -- could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why
annotations.rationale:
I can understand the statement, but I can also understand why someone would view the post as harmful. As someone who immigrated, I believe there should be respect for the culture of the place you’re moving to, as well as an understanding of why residents may want to preserve traditions and aspects of their culture.

At the same time, there should still be room for free expression, and people should be able to be themselves

annotations.tweet_text: Demographic change at this pace isn't natural. Someone is choosing this.
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous -- could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why
annotations.rationale: This was unclear to me. I couldn't really pinpoint who this was for. If I had to guess it's about either an increase in demographics because of immigration, or a decrease due to the growing LGBTQ community. I've heard both types of comments, those are the only interpretations I'd have. If it isn't about any of those topics, then I have no idea. I guess that's why I wouldn't be quick to judge.

annotations.tweet_text: Chain migration turns one visa into fifty. That's not the deal Americans signed up for.
annotations.participant_label: Likely harmful -- framing that would harm most readers from the targeted group, even if deniable
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale:
This comment comes across as, ‘We said we would help a few people, but we don’t want to go overboard and have too many people from other countries living here.’

It’s clearly directed toward immigrants. Whether the immigration is legal or not almost feels secondary, because the statement generalizes the idea that Americans are only willing to accept immigration up to a certain limit. In this context, that ‘limit’ refers to allowing immigrants and their families to build a life there.

annotations.tweet_text: Every nation has the right to exist as a distinct people. Even European ones.
annotations.participant_label: Not harmful -- policy concern, cultural commentary, or frustration with no hateful subtext
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale: I would even interpret this as something positive. Not everyone has to follow the same religion, speak the same language, or share the same beliefs. Of course, there needs to be some level of common understanding in order for people to communicate and live together effectively. But beyond that, everyone should have the freedom to be their own person and hold their own beliefs

annotations.tweet_text: We keep importing poverty and then wonder why poverty doesn't go away.
annotations.participant_label: Clearly harmful -- targets a group in a way that dehumanises or incites
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale:
This is directed toward people who immigrate in order to build a better life for themselves and their families. Many immigrants move in search of opportunities and wages they may not have access to in their home countries.

The fact that some come from more humble beginnings is being used to portray immigration as something that causes decline or negatively impacts the country accepting them

so it can be harmful but I don't feel like it attacks immigrants directly

annotations.tweet_text: The people most affected by immigration policy are the working class, not politicians.
annotations.participant_label: Ambiguous -- could be read as harmful or legitimate depending on who is reading and why
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale:
I understand that sudden demographic changes in a country can create challenges or pressures within society and the economy. So I can understand why some people feel there can be noticeable effects.

This post seems more focused on acknowledging those concerns and criticizing politicians for their policy decisions, since they are ultimately the ones responsible for shaping the system. If the system is not working effectively, the responsibility falls on them. Because of that, I wouldn’t necessarily say the post is directly attacking immigrants themselves
